etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English general, in turn from Anglo-Norman general, generall, Middle French general, and their source, Latin generālis, from genus (“class, kind”) + -ālis (“-al”); thus morphologically parallel with, and a doublet of, generic.

definitions.definition: Including or involving every part or member of a given or implied entity, whole, etc.; common to all, universal. [from 13th c.]

quote.citation: c. 1495, John Skelton, "Vppon a deedman's hed":
quote.text: It is generall / To be mortall: / I haue well espyde / No man may hym hyde / From Deth holow eyed  […] .

quote.citation: 1842, Douglas Jerrold, “Mr Peppersorn ‘At Home’”, in Cakes and Ale:
quote.text: "Among us!" was the general shout, and Peppersorn sat frozen to his chair.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XLVI, page 69:
quote.text: That each, who seems a separate whole,Should move his rounds, and fusing allThe skirts of self again, should fallRemerging in the general Soul,Is faith as vague as all unsweet:  […]

quote.citation: 1946, Bertrand Russell, “Stoicism”, in History of Western Philosophy, book 1, part 3:
quote.text: Undoubtedly the age of the Antonines was much better than any later age until the Renaissance, from the point of view of the general happiness.

quote.citation: 2006 October 15, Ruth Sutherland, “Invite public to the private equity party”, in The Observer:
quote.text: One advantage of having profitable companies in Britain is that they pay large sums in corporate tax into the Exchequer, which in theory at least is used for the general good.

definitions.definition: (sometimes postpositive) Applied to a person (as a postmodifier or a normal preceding adjective) to indicate supreme rank, in civil or military titles, and later in other terms; pre-eminent. [from 14th c.]

quote.citation: 1865, Edward Cust, Lives of the Warriors of the Thirty Years War, page 527:
quote.text: For these successes he obtained the rank of Field-Marshal General.

quote.citation: 2002, James Turner, Libertines and Radicals in Early Modern London, page 122:
quote.text: He becomes the chief chartered libertine, the whoremaster-general flourishing his "standard" over a female army  […] .

definitions.definition: Prevalent or widespread among a given class or area; common, usual. [from 14th c.]

quote.citation: 1817, Sir Walter Scott, chapter IX, in Rob Roy:
quote.text: ‘I can't quite afford you the sympathy you expect upon this score,’ I replied; ‘the misfortune is so general, that it belongs to one half of the species  […] .’

quote.citation: 2008 December 20, John Patterson, “Home movies”, in The Guardian:
quote.text: The general opinion on Baz Luhrmann's overstuffed epic Australia seems to be that it throws in everything but the kitchen sink, and then tosses that in too, just to be sure.

definitions.definition: Not limited in use or application; applicable across a broad range. [from 14th c.]

quote.text: M. Venizelos went to Athens from Paris early last January in response to a general invitation from the Greek populace.

Already in the primary school work is conducted for the purpose of equipping the pupils with those elements of general knowledge which are closely related to the military preparation of future warriors.

quote.citation: 2009, Douglas P. Zipes, Saturday Evening Post, volume 281, number 1, page 20:
quote.text: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) is a general term indicating a rapid heartbeat (tachycardia) coming from the top chambers of the heart - in essence, above (supra) the lower chamber (ventricular).

definitions.definition: Giving or consisting of only the most important aspects of something, ignoring minor details; indefinite. [from 16th c.]

quote.citation: 1817, Sir Walter Scott, chapter X, in Rob Roy:
quote.text: As she thus spoke, the entrance of the servants with dinner cut off all conversation but that of a general nature.

quote.citation: 1941, W Somerset Maugham, Up at the Villa, Vintage, published 2004, page 24:
quote.text: There was a moment's pause. The Princess broke in with some casual remark and once more the conversation became general.

quote.citation: 2006 July 16, Kevin Nance, “Ghosts of the White City”, in Chicago Sun-Times:
quote.text: The quick answer is that the 1893 Exposition was simply so important — "the greatest event in the history of the country since the Civil War," as Harper's put it that October — but that feels too general.

quote.citation: 2008, Robert P. Maloney, “The Quiet Carpenter”, in America, volume 199, number 19, page 18:
quote.text: Given the scarcity of relevant historical detail in the New Testament, we are left with only a general outline about Joseph.

definitions.definition: Not of a specific class; miscellaneous. [from 16th c.]

quote.citation: 2007, Alan Cheuse, “A Little Death”, in Southern Review, volume 43, number 3, page 692:
quote.text: His measured, springless walk was the walk of the skilled countryman as distinct from the desultory shamble of the general labourer  […] .

definitions.definition: (military) The holder of a senior military title, originally designating the commander of an army and now a specific rank falling under field marshal (in the British army) and below general of the army or general of the air force in the US army and air forces. [from 16th c.]
A great strategist or tactician. [from 16th c.]
(now rare) A general fact or proposition; a generality. [from 16th c.]
(Christianity) The head of certain religious orders, especially Dominicans or Jesuits. [from 16th c.]
(nautical) A commander of naval forces; an admiral. [16th–18th c.]
(colloquial, now historical) A general servant; a maid with no specific duties. [from 19th c.]

quote.citation: 1918 March, Rebecca West [pseudonym; Cicily Isabel Fairfield], chapter I, in The Return of the Soldier, 1st US edition, New York, N.Y.: The Century Co., →OCLC, page 18:
quote.text: My general is sister to your second housemaid.

definitions.definition: (xiangqi) A xiangqi piece that is moved one point orthogonally and confined within the palace.
(obsolete) In a general or collective manner or sense; in most cases; upon the whole.
